component.name: Splat Worker
component.summary: Train Gaussian splats for your Mac on this NVIDIA GPU

description.p: Splat Worker turns a Linux computer with an NVIDIA graphics card into a training server for Splat Studio on macOS. The Mac finds it automatically on the local network and sends it Gaussian-splat training and dataset processing jobs.

ul.li: One switch to start and stop the server
Guided setup that downloads the right PyTorch and gsplat build for your driver
Live GPU memory, temperature and utilisation
Job list with progress, PSNR, splat count and time remaining
Access token, Bonjour discovery and step-by-step help for connecting the Mac

description.p: Training requires an NVIDIA GPU (8 GB of video memory or more recommended) with a recent proprietary driver. The first-run setup downloads about 3 GB.

screenshot.caption: Server status with the GPU card and connection details
First-run setup of the GPU runtime

description.p: Fix: very large training sets (e.g. a 360° video cut into ~10,000 views) no longer exhaust the PC's memory. Images stay on the GPU when small, in RAM once when they fit, and otherwise are read from disk as needed into a bounded cache with background decoding — instead of a second, unswappable copy of every image that froze the PC part-way through training.
Result downloads can leave out nested folders (e.g. the camera solve's copy of the images), so a camera solve on a worker that already holds the frames sends back only cameras and points.

Much faster camera solving for 360° video: views of the same 360° frame are matched and placed together as one camera rig with their known directions and lens, and mapped globally. On 60 frames (960 views) of a walk: every view placed, mapping in 2 minutes instead of 7, about a third as many image pairs to match.
A PC on both ethernet and Wi-Fi announces its ethernet address first (and lists all addresses with their kind), so Splat Studio connects over the cable when it can.
Experimental training options: coarse-to-fine image resolution (progressiveResolution) and decoupled SSIM for per-photo colour correction (decoupledSSIM).

Fix: camera solving with SuperPoint/ALIKED/DISK + LightGlue failed after matching with "no SfM mapper available" on workers without the COLMAP program, although pycolmap was installed. A missing mapper is now reported before matching starts.
Processing results stay on the worker for the next step: a video split here is masked, solved and trained here without its frames going back and forth to the Mac (gigabytes for 360° video).
Trained splats record the scene's up direction, so drone and other Z-up scenes open the right way up in Splat Studio.
Optional per-photo local colour correction (bilateralGrid): lets each photo have its own shadows and lighting, for long drone flights where the sun moves between shots.
Per-photo colour correction switches off when every photo has the same exposure (iPhone captures with locked exposure), which improved held-out quality by about 1 dB on a bedroom scan.
Set Up uses a gsplat wheel built on this PC (linux/flatpak/build-gsplat-wheel.sh) when there is one, so the gsplat 1.6 runtime no longer has to wait for the published build.

Long-axis splitting is on by default: training no longer collapses on large scenes once the splat budget fills. iPhone capture poses are refined (look-at pairs, pose-only bundle adjustment with pycolmap) instead of re-solved, and GPS-tagged photo sets are checked against GPS and put in metres with Z up.

Set Up only picks a GPU runtime whose packages are actually published (the gsplat 1.6 build is checked first), and builds the new runtime next to the old one, swapping it in only after it passes its check — a failed or cancelled setup no longer breaks a working worker.
Watching a job from the Mac now shows that job's own cameras (new /v1/jobs/{id}/cameras), not the cameras of whatever project is open.

Splits videos (including 8K 360° footage) on the worker: the Mac streams the video up unchanged and gets the frames and views back. Needs the processing models (adds PyAV). Camera solving keeps EXIF focal lengths fixed, fixing flat drone surveys.

New GPU runtime: PyTorch 2.7 + CUDA 12.8 with a development build of gsplat 1.6 (drivers 570+), which also adds RTX 50-series support. Older drivers keep the gsplat 1.5.3 runtime. Run Set Up… to switch.
Experimental long-axis splitting for MCMC training (off by default).
Fix: the needle-splat penalty also squashed flat, disc-shaped splats (the normal shape on surfaces), giving faint, painterly results. It now only targets genuine needles.
Reports training and held-out PSNR separately, so Splat Studio's charts no longer switch metrics mid-run.
Experimental per-photo camera pose refinement (off by default).
Fix: the needle-splat penalty could make long High-quality runs diverge; it now only shortens long splats.
Processing models: transformers pinned to releases that work with this runtime (Python 3.10, PyTorch 2.4); setup checks that torchvision actually loads.
Fix: installing the processing models could replace the GPU runtime's PyTorch, breaking training. Run Set Up… again to repair an affected install.
Install processing models remotely from Splat Studio; edge-aware depth, needle-splat penalty, and moving-object masking that switches off for sparse captures.
Optional processing models (COLMAP mapper, OWLv2, SAM 2) so Splat Studio can run camera solving and moving-object masking on this GPU.
Per-photo colour correction, live previews for Splat Studio, update notifications, and a fix for block-parallel training.
First Flatpak release with a desktop interface and guided GPU setup.
